purpose: 本报告全部规范引文：逐条可点开核验 + 独立对抗复核判词。
method: 每份来源由独立 agent 实取原文，再由另一个独立 agent 尝试证伪（verbatim / official / supports 三项）。

confirmed.version: NIST Special Publication 800-38A, 2001 Edition, "Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Methods and Techniques", Morris Dworkin, December 2001 (PDF CreationDate 2001-12-10; 66 pages)

quotes.text: The Electronic Codebook (ECB) mode is a confidentiality mode that features, for a given key, the assignment of a fixed ciphertext block to each plaintext block, analogous to the assignment of code words in a codebook.
quotes.locator: §6.1 The Electronic Codebook Mode, printed p. 9 (PDF p. 16), opening sentence
quotes.supports: (a) fixed ciphertext block assigned to each plaintext block under a given key

quotes.text: In the ECB mode, under a given key, any given plaintext block always gets encrypted to the same ciphertext block.
quotes.locator: §6.1 The Electronic Codebook Mode, printed pp. 9-10 (PDF pp. 16-17); sentence spans the page break
quotes.supports: (a) the exact determinism sentence: any given plaintext block always encrypts to the same ciphertext block

quotes.text: If this property is undesirable in a particular application, the ECB mode should not be used.
quotes.locator: §6.1 The Electronic Codebook Mode, printed p. 10 (PDF p. 17)
quotes.supports: closest thing in SP 800-38A to an ECB suitability warning — conditional on the determinism property being undesirable, NOT a diffusion or short-data statement

quotes.text: In ECB encryption, the forward cipher function is applied directly and independently to each block of the plaintext.
quotes.locator: §6.1 The Electronic Codebook Mode, printed p. 9 (PDF p. 16)
quotes.supports: ECB blocks are enciphered independently — the mechanism behind the determinism property

confirmed.key: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 — Recommendation for Key Management: Part 1 – General (Elaine Barker, May 2020)
confirmed.version: NIST Special Publication 800-57 Part 1, Revision 5, May 2020 (170 pages; PDF has 171 pages). DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-57pt1r5. SHA-256 of the downloaded file: cc32391022c1382ac7c91490f6bcc8838e0f889925270da23ef4e800e2ecb7ad. Landing page confirmed at https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-57-part-1/rev-5/final (final version dated 05/04/20).

quotes.text: Information protected by cryptographic mechanisms is secure only if the algorithms remain strong and the keys have not been compromised. It is the responsibility of an owner of a private or secret key to protect the confidentiality of that key. Key compromise occurs when the protective mechanisms for the key fail (e.g., the confidentiality, integrity, or association of the key to its owner fail; see Section 6) and the key can no longer be trusted to provide the required security.
quotes.locator: Section 5.5 "Compromise of Keys and other Keying Material", opening paragraph — printed p. 49 (PDF p. 62)
quotes.supports: Definition of key compromise and the owner's duty to protect key confidentiality (the frame for any 'key shipped inside the product' argument)

quotes.text: When a key is compromised, all use of the key to apply cryptographic protection to information (e.g., compute a digital signature or encrypt information) shall cease, and the compromised key shall be revoked (see Section 8.3.5).
quotes.locator: Section 5.5, second paragraph — printed p. 49 (PDF p. 62)
quotes.supports: (c) compromise mandates ceasing use and revoking the key

quotes.text: The continued use of a compromised key shall be limited to processing information that has already been protected.
quotes.locator: Section 5.5, third paragraph — printed p. 49 (PDF p. 62)
quotes.supports: (c) the only permitted residual use of a compromised key is verifying/decrypting already-protected data

quotes.text: The worst form of key compromise is one that is not detected. Nevertheless, even in this case, certain protective measures can be taken. A key management system should be designed to mitigate the negative effects of a key compromise; the system should be designed so that the compromise of a single key compromises as little data as possible (see SP 800-152). For example, a single cryptographic key could be used to protect the data of only a single human entity or a limited number of such entities. Often, systems have alternative methods to authenticate communicating entities that do not rely solely on the possession of keys. The intent is to avoid building a system with catastrophic weaknesses.
quotes.locator: Section 5.5.2 "Protective Measures", closing paragraph — printed p. 51 (PDF p. 64)
quotes.supports: Blast-radius principle: one key must not be shared fleet-wide; a single shared key makes one compromise catastrophic

quotes.text: The following procedures are usually involved: 1. Limiting the amount of time that a secret symmetric or asymmetric private key is in plaintext form; 2. Preventing humans from viewing plaintext secret symmetric and asymmetric private keys; 3. Restricting plaintext secret and private keys to physically protected “containers.” This includes key generators, key-transport devices, key loaders, cryptographic modules, hardware security modules (HSMs), and key-storage devices;
quotes.locator: Section 5.5.2 "Protective Measures", items 1–3 — printed p. 50 (PDF p. 63)
quotes.supports: (a) closest thing in this document to 'do not leave keys exposed in the application': plaintext key material must be confined to physically protected containers, and humans must not be able to view it

quotes.text: Generally, keys are compromised when they are provided to or determined by an unauthorized entity. A compromised key shall not be used to apply cryptographic protection to information.
quotes.locator: Section 7.5 "Compromised State" — printed p. 87 (PDF p. 100)
quotes.supports: (c) the state machine view: once provided to an unauthorized entity the key is in the compromised state and shall not protect data

quotes.text: The security of keying-material installation is crucial to the security of a system, whether the keying material is generated within the system (e.g., in the system’s cryptographic module) or generated within another system and subsequently installed in the (target) system. For this function, keying material is installed for operational use within an entity’s software, hardware, system, application, cryptographic module, or device using a variety of techniques.
quotes.locator: Section 8.1.4 "Keying-Material Installation Function", opening paragraph — printed p. 92 (PDF p. 105)
quotes.supports: (a) key material installed into an application/device is explicitly in scope and its security is called 'crucial'

quotes.text: The process for the initial installation of keying material (e.g., by manual entry, using an electronic key loader, or a vendor during manufacture) shall include the protection of the keying material during entry into a software, hardware, system, application, device, or cryptographic module
quotes.locator: Section 8.1.4, second paragraph — printed p. 92 (PDF p. 105)
quotes.supports: (a) installation 'during manufacture' into 'software, hardware, system, application, device' carries a shall-level protection requirement

quotes.text: Many applications or systems are provided by the manufacturer with keying material that is used to test that the newly installed application/system is functioning properly. This test keying material shall not be used operationally.
quotes.locator: Section 8.1.4, final paragraph — printed p. 92 (PDF p. 105)
quotes.supports: (a) vendor-shipped embedded key material is expressly forbidden from operational use — the nearest explicit rule about baked-in keys in this document

quotes.text: Confidentiality protection shall be provided for all secret key information (i.e., key information that is intended to be kept secret, such as symmetric (secret) keys, asymmetric private keys, key shares, and secret metadata).
quotes.locator: Section 6.1 "Protection and Assurance Requirements", first requirement — printed p. 65 (PDF p. 78)
quotes.supports: (a) all secret keys require confidentiality protection, with no carve-out for keys bundled in an app

quotes.text: When the secret or private key information is available outside of a cryptographic module, confidentiality protection shall be provided by encryption at an appropriate security strength (see SP 800-152) or by controlling access to the secret key information via physical means.
quotes.locator: Section 6.1, first requirement, final sentence — printed p. 65 (PDF p. 78)
quotes.supports: (a) a key living outside a cryptographic module must still be encrypted or physically access-controlled — a bare string in an app satisfies neither

quotes.text: One of the following mechanisms shall be used to provide confidentiality for secret key information in storage: 1. Encryption (or key wrapping) using an approved algorithm in a FIPS 140-validated cryptographic module; the encryption shall use an approved technique that provides protection at the security strength that meets or exceeds the security strength required for the secret key information. -OR- 2. Physical protection provided by a FIPS 140-validated cryptographic module at a security level that is consistent with the FIPS 199 impact level associated with the data to be protected by the key (see SP 800-152). -OR- 3. Physical protection provided by secure storage with controlled access (e.g., a safe or protected area).
quotes.locator: Section 6.2.2.3 "Confidentiality" — printed p. 77 (PDF p. 90)
quotes.supports: (a) exhaustive three-option list for at-rest secret keys; a key embedded in application code matches none of the three

quotes.text: When keying material is compromised, continuity of operations requires the establishment of entirely new keying material (see Section 8.1.5) following an assessment of the keying material that was affected; all affected keying material needs to be replaced.
quotes.locator: Section 8.2.2 "Continuity of Operations Function", second paragraph — printed p. 105 (PDF p. 118)
quotes.supports: (c) compromise requires establishment of entirely new keying material and replacement of all affected material

quotes.text: Re-keying is used when a key has been compromised (provided that the re-keying scheme itself is not compromised) or when the cryptoperiod has expired or is nearing expiration.
quotes.locator: Section 8.2.3.1 "Re-keying" — printed p. 108 (PDF p. 121)
quotes.supports: (c) the replacement mechanism for a compromised key is re-keying via key establishment

quotes.text: If a key is compromised, its cryptoperiod shall no longer be considered valid.
quotes.locator: Section 5.3 "Cryptoperiods", second paragraph — printed p. 34 (PDF p. 47)
quotes.supports: (c) compromise invalidates the key's authorized lifetime

quotes.text: A key may be revoked for administrative reasons (e.g., the key’s owner has left the organization, or a device containing the key has been removed from service), or it may be revoked on an emergency basis if there is reason to believe that it may have been disclosed to or otherwise accessed by an unauthorized entity. In either case, a cryptographic key should be revoked as soon as feasible after the need for revocation has been determined.
quotes.locator: Section 8.3.5 "Key Revocation Function", opening paragraph — printed p. 113 (PDF p. 126)
quotes.supports: (c) revocation triggers include suspected disclosure, and revocation should follow as soon as feasible

quotes.text: Key establishment is the process by which cryptographic keys are securely established among entities using manual transport methods (e.g., key loaders), automated methods (e.g., key-transport and/or key-agreement protocols), or a combination of automated and manual methods.
quotes.locator: Section 3.6 "Support Services" — printed p. 23 (PDF p. 36); identical wording also in the Section 2.1 glossary entry "Key establishment" (printed p. 12, PDF p. 25)
quotes.supports: (b) formal definition of key establishment vs. a key that is simply pre-placed

quotes.text: Static key A key that is intended for use for a relatively long period of time and is typically intended for use in many instances of a cryptographic key-establishment scheme. Contrast with an Ephemeral key.
quotes.locator: Section 2.1 "Glossary", entry "Static key" — printed p. 19 (PDF p. 32)
quotes.supports: (b) glossary definition of a static (long-term) key and its contrast with ephemeral keys

quotes.text: Ephemeral keys are often used for key agreement instead of or in addition to the use of static keys (see SP 800-56A).
quotes.locator: Section 8.1.5.1 "Generation and Distribution of Asymmetric Key Pairs" — printed p. 93 (PDF p. 106)
quotes.supports: (b) ephemeral-vs-static tradeoff in key agreement

quotes.text: Ephemeral key pairs are generated for each new key-establishment transaction (e.g., unique to each message or session) by the owner.
quotes.locator: Section 8.1.5.1, paragraph on ephemeral key pairs — printed p. 93 (PDF p. 106)
quotes.supports: (b) per-session freshness that a shipped static key cannot provide

quotes.text: A key-agreement scheme uses either static or ephemeral asymmetric key pairs or both.
quotes.locator: Section 8.1.5.2.3 "Key Agreement" — printed p. 101 (PDF p. 114)
quotes.supports: (b) key agreement can rest on static or ephemeral key pairs

quotes.text: Key update could result in a security exposure if an adversary obtains a key in the chain of derived keys and knows the update process that was used; keys subsequent to the compromised key could easily be determined.
quotes.locator: Section 8.2.3.2 "Key Update Function" — printed p. 108 (PDF p. 121)
quotes.supports: (c) derived/updated keys inherit compromise from a single leaked predecessor key

quotes.text: The number of nodes in a network that share a common key;
quotes.locator: Section 5.3.1 "Factors Affecting Cryptoperiods", item 11 — printed p. 35 (PDF p. 48)
quotes.supports: (a) NIST treats the population sharing one key as a cryptoperiod-shortening risk factor

quotes.text: In general, where strong cryptography is employed, physical, procedural, and logical access-protection considerations often have more impact on cryptoperiod selection than do algorithm and key-size factors.
quotes.locator: Section 5.3.1, closing paragraph — printed p. 35 (PDF p. 48)
quotes.supports: (a) access protection around the key matters more than algorithm strength

quotes.text: adversaries may be able to access keys through the penetration or subversion of a system with less expenditure of time and resources than would be required to mount and execute a cryptographic attack.
quotes.locator: Section 5.3.1, closing paragraph, final sentence — printed p. 35 (PDF p. 48)
quotes.supports: (a) key extraction via subverting the system is cheaper than cryptanalysis — the core rationale against shipping keys in the client

quotes.text: Trust-anchor certificates are often embedded within an application and distributed with the application.
quotes.locator: Section 8.1.5.1.1 "Distribution of a Trust Anchor’s Public Key in a PKI" — printed p. 94 (PDF p. 107)
quotes.supports: Only use of 'embedded' in the whole document; it refers to public trust-anchor certificates, not secret keys

quotes.text: In some cases, the costs associated with changing keys are painfully high. Examples include the decryption and subsequent re-encryption of very large databases, the decryption and re-encryption of distributed databases, and the revocation and replacement of a very large number of keys (e.g., where there are very large numbers of geographically and organizationally distributed key holders).
quotes.locator: Section 5.3.3.2 "Cost of Key Revocation and Replacement" — printed p. 36 (PDF p. 49)
quotes.supports: (c) why replacing a widely distributed key is expensive — the operational cost of the mandated replacement

quotes.text: The unauthorized disclosure of a key means that another entity (an unauthorized entity) may know the key and be able to use that key to perform computations requiring the use of the key.
quotes.locator: Section 5.5.1 "Implications", item 1 — printed p. 49 (PDF p. 62)
quotes.supports: (c) consequence of disclosure: an unauthorized party can perform the key's computations

quotes.text: The security of encrypted information that was available at any time to unauthorized entities in its encrypted form should be considered suspect.
quotes.locator: Section 5.6.5 "Decrease of Security Strength Over Time", first bullet — printed p. 63 (PDF p. 76)
quotes.supports: (c) retroactive damage: previously protected data must be treated as suspect after compromise

confirmed.version: OWASP MASVS v2.1.0 (latest release, tagged 2024-01-18; control text byte-identical on master HEAD bbe226fd17e6 dated 2026-09-21 and on tag v2.0.0). MASTG v2.0.0 (release tag 2026-06-30; test sources live under tests-beta/ on master HEAD 2eb0f7097e5f dated 2026-10-24).

quotes.text: The app employs current strong cryptography and uses it according to industry best practices.
quotes.locator: MASVS-CRYPTO-1 — Control (statement); https://mas.owasp.org/MASVS/controls/MASVS-CRYPTO-1/ and controls/MASVS-CRYPTO-1.md on tag v2.1.0
quotes.supports: Exact requirement statement text for MASVS-CRYPTO-1

quotes.text: Cryptography plays an especially important role in securing the user's data - even more so in a mobile environment, where attackers having physical access to the user's device is a likely scenario. This control covers general cryptography best practices, which are typically defined in external standards.
quotes.locator: MASVS-CRYPTO-1 — Description; https://mas.owasp.org/MASVS/controls/MASVS-CRYPTO-1/
quotes.supports: CRYPTO-1 elaboration: general crypto best practices, external standards (NIST)

quotes.text: The app performs key management according to industry best practices.
quotes.locator: MASVS-CRYPTO-2 — Control (statement); https://mas.owasp.org/MASVS/controls/MASVS-CRYPTO-2/ and controls/MASVS-CRYPTO-2.md on tag v2.1.0
quotes.supports: Exact requirement statement text for MASVS-CRYPTO-2

quotes.text: Even the strongest cryptography would be compromised by poor key management. This control covers the management of cryptographic keys throughout their lifecycle, including key generation, storage and protection.
quotes.locator: MASVS-CRYPTO-2 — Description; https://mas.owasp.org/MASVS/controls/MASVS-CRYPTO-2/
quotes.supports: CRYPTO-2 elaboration on key storage / key management / key lifecycle

quotes.text: This category also focuses on the management of cryptographic keys throughout their lifecycle, including key generation, storage, and protection. Poor key management can compromise even the strongest cryptography, so it is crucial for developers to follow the recommended best practices to ensure the security of their users' sensitive data.
quotes.locator: MASVS-CRYPTO: Cryptography — chapter introduction; https://mas.owasp.org/MASVS/06-MASVS-CRYPTO/ and Document/06-MASVS-CRYPTO.md
quotes.supports: Category-level framing that CRYPTO-2 owns key storage/key management

quotes.text: The purpose of the controls in this category is to ensure that the verified app uses cryptography according to industry best practices, which are typically defined in external standards such as [NIST.SP.800-175B](...) and [NIST.SP.800-57](...).
quotes.locator: MASVS-CRYPTO: Cryptography — chapter introduction; https://mas.owasp.org/MASVS/06-MASVS-CRYPTO/
quotes.supports: Which external standards the MASVS-CRYPTO controls point to

quotes.text: The test case fails if you find any hardcoded keys that are used in security-sensitive contexts.
quotes.locator: MASTG-TEST-0212 — Evaluation; https://mas.owasp.org/MASTG/tests/android/MASVS-CRYPTO/MASTG-TEST-0212/ (source: tests-beta/android/MASVS-CRYPTO/MASTG-TEST-0212.md)
quotes.supports: Current MASTG test and pass/fail criterion for hardcoded keys (Android)

quotes.text: In this test case, we will look for the use of hardcoded keys in Android applications. To do this, we need to focus on the cryptographic implementations of hardcoded keys. The Java Cryptography Architecture (JCA) provides the SecretKeySpec class, which allows you to create a SecretKey from a byte array.
quotes.locator: MASTG-TEST-0212 — Overview; title: "Use of Hardcoded Cryptographic Keys in Code"
quotes.supports: MASTG-TEST-0212 scope and the Android API of interest

quotes.text: The test case fails if calls to cryptographic functions with hardcoded keys are found within binary.
quotes.locator: MASTG-TEST-0213 — Evaluation; https://mas.owasp.org/MASTG/tests/ios/MASVS-CRYPTO/MASTG-TEST-0213/ (source: tests-beta/ios/MASVS-CRYPTO/MASTG-TEST-0213.md)
quotes.supports: Current MASTG test and pass/fail criterion for hardcoded keys (iOS)

quotes.text: In this test case, we will examine iOS applications for the presence of hardcoded cryptographic keys. Hardcoded keys can be typically found in calls to cryptographic functions or stored as constants or variables within the code.
quotes.locator: MASTG-TEST-0213 — Overview; title: "Use of Hardcoded Cryptographic Keys in Code"
quotes.supports: MASTG-TEST-0213 scope (iOS hardcoded keys)

quotes.text: You may find the keys being directly passed as arguments to cryptographic functions (byte arrays or string literals) or stored in variables or constants within the code. Typical representations of hardcoded keys include: - Raw Byte Arrays: ... - Base64-Encoded Strings: ... - Hex-Encoded Strings: ...
quotes.locator: MASTG-TEST-0213 — Evaluation (iOS)
quotes.supports: Concrete forms hardcoded symmetric keys take in binaries

quotes.text: A common mistake is encrypting locally stored data with a static, hardcoded encryption key and compiling that key into the app. This makes the key accessible to anyone who can use a disassembler.
quotes.locator: MASTG Document/0x04g-Testing-Cryptography.md — section "Symmetric Encryption with Hard-Coded Cryptographic Keys"
quotes.supports: Official MASTG rationale for why hardcoded keys are a finding

quotes.text: Hardcoded encryption key means that a key is: - part of application resources - value which can be derived from known values - hardcoded in code
quotes.locator: MASTG Document/0x04g-Testing-Cryptography.md — section "Symmetric Encryption with Hard-Coded Cryptographic Keys"
quotes.supports: Official three-part definition of a hardcoded encryption key

quotes.text: Secret keys must be stored in secure device storage whenever symmetric cryptography is used in mobile apps.
quotes.locator: MASTG Document/0x04g-Testing-Cryptography.md — section "Symmetric Encryption with Hard-Coded Cryptographic Keys"
quotes.supports: Key-storage requirement that pairs with MASVS-CRYPTO-2

quotes.text: For each identified instance verify if the used symmetric keys: - are not part of the application resources - cannot be derived from known values - are not hardcoded in code
quotes.locator: MASTG-TEST-0013 — Static Analysis (status: deprecated, covered_by MASTG-TEST-0212, MASTG-TEST-0221, MASTG-TEST-0309, MASTG-TEST-0310)
quotes.supports: The older v1 symmetric-cryptography test that carried the hardcoded-key checks

quotes.text: This test is deprecated and should not be used anymore. Reason: Please check the following MASTG v2 tests that cover this v1 test: Use of Hardcoded Cryptographic Keys in Code / Broken Symmetric Encryption Algorithms / References to Reused Initialization Vectors in Symmetric Encryption / Runtime Use of Reused Initialization Vectors in Symmetric Encryption
quotes.locator: https://mas.owasp.org/MASTG/tests/android/MASVS-CRYPTO/MASTG-TEST-0013/ — "Deprecated Test" banner
quotes.supports: MASTG-TEST-0013 is retired; its hardcoded-key content now lives in MASTG-TEST-0212

quotes.text: This weakness occurs when cryptographic keys are stored outside the platform-provided secure keystore, in locations such as unencrypted preferences, unprotected files, or the application code itself.
quotes.locator: MASWE-0003 "Cryptographic Keys Stored Outside of Platform Keystore" — Overview; weaknesses/MASVS-STORAGE/MASWE-0003.md; requirement: "The app stores cryptographic keys inside the platform-provided secure keystore." (masvs-v2: [MASVS-STORAGE-1, MASVS-CRYPTO-2])
quotes.supports: The MASWE weakness that maps MASVS-CRYPTO-2 to hardcoded / improperly stored keys

quotes.text: This weakness occurs when cryptographic keys can be used without restrictions on who may use them, under which device conditions, and for how long.
quotes.locator: MASWE-0016 "Cryptographic Key Access Not Restricted" — Overview; requirement: "The app restricts access to cryptographic keys." (masvs-v2: [MASVS-CRYPTO-2, MASVS-AUTH-2, MASVS-AUTH-3])
quotes.supports: Second MASWE weakness under MASVS-CRYPTO-2 covering key access restrictions

quotes.text: Defense-in-depth measures such as code obfuscation, anti-debugging, anti-tampering, and runtime application self-protection (RASP) can increase an app's resilience against reverse engineering and specific client-side attacks.
quotes.locator: MASVS-RESILIENCE group introduction, Document/11-MASVS-RESILIENCE.md (master) and live https://mas.owasp.org/MASVS/11-MASVS-RESILIENCE/ — first sentence under the group title
quotes.supports: Obfuscation is named as an EXAMPLE of a defense-in-depth measure, not as a requirement

quotes.text: The absence of these measures does not in itself constitute a vulnerability. Instead, resilience controls provide additional protection against threat-specific attacks. All apps must also fulfill the rest of the OWASP MASVS controls according to their threat model.
quotes.locator: MASVS-RESILIENCE group introduction, Document/11-MASVS-RESILIENCE.md (master), lines 5 — rendered on live site with the first and third sentences in bold
quotes.supports: The exact wording establishing that missing resilience measures are NOT a vulnerability — i.e. not mandatory

quotes.text: However, note that the lack of any of these measures does not necessarily cause vulnerabilities - instead, they add threat-specific additional protection to apps which must also fulfil the rest of the OWASP MASVS security controls according to their specific threat models.
quotes.locator: OWASP_MASVS.yaml, group MASVS-RESILIENCE (index 7), 'description' field — master branch
quotes.supports: Machine-readable source states the same non-mandatory framing; this is the v2.1.0-era wording that also appears in the v2.1.0 group intro

quotes.text: some testers report a lack of obfuscation or root detection in an Android app as “security flaw”. On the other hand, measures like string encryption, debugger detection or control flow obfuscation aren't considered mandatory. However, this binary way of looking at things doesn't make sense because resilience is not a binary proposition: It depends on the particular client-side threats one aims to defend against.
quotes.locator: Document/01-Foreword.md, fifth-from-last paragraph before the "The overall goal of the MASVS" paragraph (Bernhard Mueller)
quotes.supports: Strongest single statement that obfuscation is explicitly NOT mandatory, and that calling its absence a 'security flaw' is criticized by OWASP

quotes.text: The overall goal of the MASVS is to offer a baseline for mobile application security, while also allowing for the inclusion of defense-in-depth measures and protections against client-side threats.
quotes.locator: Document/01-Foreword.md, paragraph beginning "The overall goal of the MASVS"
quotes.supports: Resilience/obfuscation sit in the defense-in-depth layer, additional to the baseline

quotes.text: Software protections are not useless, but they can ultimately be bypassed, so they must never be used as a replacement for security controls.
quotes.locator: Document/01-Foreword.md, same paragraph as the "aren't considered mandatory" sentence
quotes.supports: Why obfuscation cannot be a mandatory control: it is bypassable and cannot substitute for real controls

quotes.text: Anti-tampering or obfuscation techniques must not be used as a substitute for proper security architecture
quotes.locator: Document/11-MASVS-RESILIENCE.md, section "Transparency and Open Audit Perspective", bullet list of recommended principles
quotes.supports: OWASP affirmatively argues obfuscation may be undesirable for public-interest apps and is never a substitute for architecture

quotes.text: Note that the absence of any MAS-R measures does not inherently introduce vulnerabilities. Rather, these measures offer additional, threat-specific protection to applications. However, this is provided that these apps also meet the rest of the OWASP MASVS security controls appropriate to their specific threat models. Crucially, MAS-R is meant to augment and not replace MAS-L1 and MAS-L2. It should not be used standalone but as an extra layer of defense, supplementing the base security controls in a defense-in-depth strategy.

The cited URL resolves to a metadata card (`newGbInfo`) carrying only standard number, title, 现行 status, CCS L80 / ICS 35.030, 发布日期 2021-10-11, 实施日期 2022-05-01, and issuing bodies — with an EMPTY 备注. The standard's full text is served only as session-gated page images via `/bzgk/std/viewGbImg?fileName=...`, which returned 302/0 bytes on all 11 chunks. So the quotes were not, and could not have been, read from the cited URL; the '正文第N页' locators are asserted, not demonstrated. Independently verified as EXACT: 密码法 第八条/第二十四条/第二十七条 (oscca.gov.cn), 商用密码管理条例 第三十八条/第三十九条 (gov.cn gazette), and both GM/Y 5001-2021 passages with correct printed pages 10 and 18 (official gmbz.org.cn PDF). Independently CONFIRMED in substance (via the official 2023 edition of the same guide): the 9-mode list, '附录A 是资料性附录' for GB/T 17964, and '附录B 是资料性附录' for GB/T 39786 — the agent's non-normativity hedges are correct, not spin. Correctly handled: GM/Y 5001-2021 describes GB/T 17964-**2008** (7 modes); the agent did not blend that with the 2021 standard's 9 modes. Two misattributions/stretches to fix: (a) the GM/T 0054 scope quote is on neither cited page — bzgfcx.jsp has zero '0054' occurrences, and the dedicated OSCCA page carries only the title; (b) the GB/T 39786 '第5章 a)' quote appears on antpedia under a possibly site-added heading '与法规或其他标准的关系说明', so clause 5 a) is unverified; likewise the '8.4' wording reads as an interpretive summary rather than clause text. Two quotes remain unconfirmed verbatim: '密钥可以在符合 GB/T 37092 的密码产品中产生是十分必要的' and '对于超过一个分组长度的明文一般建议不使用 ECB 工作模式'. Recommended fix: re-cite the GB/T 17964 and GB/T 39786 body quotes as '原文未取得，转引自官方 GM/Y 5001（2023版）内容概要' or obtain the text via a licensed channel, and drop the '代替GB/T 17964-2008' clause from any claim attributed to this URL.
